html:
A canal about six kilometres long cut through the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece between 1881 and 1893. It links the Gulf of Corinth with the Aegean Sea and spares ships the long trip round the Peloponnese.

The idea is ancient. The tyrant Periander of Corinth thought of it around 600 BCE but built a paved track, the Diolkos, to drag ships across instead. The Roman emperor Nero began digging in 67 CE and broke the first ground with a golden shovel, but the work stopped after his death.

The modern canal was dug by a French company, with Hungarian engineers in charge. Its sheer rock walls rise high above the water, and it is only about 21 metres wide. That made it too narrow for many ships even when new, and costs and landslides hurt the company. Today it carries mostly tourist boats and small ships.

It runs close to where the Byzantines built the Hexamilion wall to defend the same narrow neck of land.
sum: A canal about six kilometres long cut through the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece between 1881 and 1893. It links the Gulf of Corinth with the Aegean Sea and spares ships the long trip round the Peloponnese.
